nature-econ-509.title: Consumption: spending to meet today's needs
nature-econ-509.text: In most countries, consumption is the largest part of GDP, usually between 45% and 85% of it. Consumption is the use of resources to meet present needs and wants, as opposed to investing for future income. Mainstream economists count only final purchases of newly produced goods and services by individuals for immediate use. In macroeconomics, consumption equals income minus savings. Economists consider income the most important factor affecting it. In microeconomics, the view is individual: consumers are assumed to choose the goods that maximize their utility within their budget. Add up everyone's consumption and you get one component of aggregate demand, the total spending in an economy.

nature-econ-491.title: Income: what you gain over a period
nature-econ-491.text: Watching a sunset is a joy, but it is not income. Income is the ability to consume and save that a person, household or firm gains over a set period, usually counted in money. Because non-monetary joys are left out, reported income may misstate well-being. Income is also hard to define, and its meaning differs between fields. Economic income can differ from income as the law defines it. US tax law, for example, counts wages, salary, profit, interest, rent and other earnings received in a calendar year as household income. For a firm, gross income can be defined as all revenue minus the cost of goods sold. Some rules hold under every definition. Borrowing or repaying money is never income, but interest and forgiven debt are. Education raises income by increasing workers' skills and productivity. Economists conventionally write income as Y. Because it is measured over a period, income is a flow, in the sense of {{ref:nature-econ-594}}.

nature-econ-499.title: Wealth: what you own minus what you owe
nature-econ-499.text: For 2018 the World Bank valued the world's produced, natural and human capital at $1,152 trillion. That is wealth counted on the widest scale. In general, wealth means a plentiful store of valuable assets or possessions that can be turned into a form usable in exchange. In economics it is net worth: the value of all assets owned minus all liabilities owed, at a point in time, for a person, household or nation. Adam Smith described wealth as 'the annual produce of the land and labor of the society'. Scarcity is fundamental. A commodity freely available to everyone gives its owner no potential for wealth. Wealth falls into three main categories: personal property, monetary savings, and income-producing capital such as real estate, stocks and businesses. Global household wealth was estimated at US$418.3 trillion at the end of 2020, excluding human capital. The UN goes further with the measure described in {{ref:nature-acct-012}}, adding up natural, human and physical assets in money terms. Natural capital includes land, forests, energy resources and minerals. Human capital is people's education and skills, and physical capital is machinery, buildings and infrastructure.

nature-econ-587.title: Saving: income held back for later
nature-econ-587.text: In a simple farming economy, saving might mean holding back the best of the corn harvest as seed for next season. Saving is income not spent on immediate consumption; in economics, it is after-tax income minus consumption. The grammar matters. Saving is an activity over time, a flow, while savings is an amount held at one moment, a stock. Saving supplies the funds for investment. Income not spent on consumer goods can build factories and machinery, which supports growth. Capital markets balance personal saving, government surpluses and net exports against physical investment. Yet more saving does not always mean more investment. It can instead cause a shortfall of demand and a recession. In personal finance, saving means low-risk preservation of money, while investment carries a higher risk of loss.

nature-econ-538.title: Investment: putting resources to work for a return
nature-econ-538.text: Modern investing is usually dated to the 17th century, and the Amsterdam Stock Exchange began in 1602. To invest is to commit resources, often money, to something expected to gain value over time. In finance, the aim is to earn a return. The return can come as a capital gain or loss when the asset is sold, or as regular income such as dividends, interest or rent. Risk and reward travel together. Investors usually expect higher returns from riskier investments, and low-risk investments generally earn low returns. Spreading money across many investments reduces overall risk. Common investments include stocks, bonds, cash, real estate, private equity and commodities. Compared with savings, they carry more kinds of risk and greater uncertainty. Much investing runs through intermediaries such as pension funds, banks and insurance companies, which pool money from many investors.

nature-econ-539.title: Investment in the national economy: adding to the capital stock
nature-econ-539.text: In a national economy, investment has a specific meaning. It is spending in a year that adds to the country's stock of buildings, equipment, software and inventories. In classical theory, it means producing goods that are not consumed right away but used to make other goods. Investment is a flow measured over a period. Capital is the stock it builds: the net investment accumulated up to a point in time. Net investment is gross investment minus depreciation, and net fixed investment is the yearly net increase in the capital stock. Investment is often modelled as falling when interest rates rise, since interest is the cost of funds, and rising with income. Some research models it as rising with the gap between the profit-maximizing capital stock and the current one. It is closely related to saving, but it is not the same thing.

nature-econ-495.title: The family of national income measures
nature-econ-495.text: Systematic national accounts began only in the 1930s, in the United States and some European countries, spurred by the Great Depression and Keynes's ideas. Out of them came a family of statistics, such as GDP, {{ref:nature-econ-530}} and {{ref:nature-econ-571}}, used to estimate the total economic activity of a country or region. All of them count the goods and services produced within an economy and its sectors. They count them at market value, the price they fetch, not their actual usefulness. Three methods give the market value of all output: the product, expenditure and income methods. Some measures count only goods and services exchanged for money, while others impute values for bartered goods. One variant, adjusted national income, corrects that net figure for the using up of resources taken from nature.

nature-econ-485.title: Adding up GDP by who does the spending
nature-econ-485.text: Economists write GDP as a sum: Y = C + I + G + (X − M). Consumption (C), households' private spending, is normally the largest part. Investment (I) means spending on things like new equipment, buildings and software. Buying shares or bonds does not count here; it counts as saving. Government spending (G) covers final goods and services such as public salaries, but not transfer payments like unemployment benefits. Exports (X) are added and imports (M) subtracted. Imports already appear inside C, I and G, and they must not be counted as domestic supply. Throughout, only spending on final goods counts. Intermediate goods used to make other products are left out.

nature-econ-545.title: Keynesian economics: when markets fail to clear
nature-econ-545.text: During the Great Depression, goods went unsold and workers stayed unemployed, and the economists of the day struggled to explain why. The older neoclassical view held that prices and wages would fall until all goods and labour were sold. Keynes's General Theory, published in 1936, began a new school of thought. Keynesian economics explains why markets might not clear, leaving goods and workers unused, and it stresses total demand as the driver of output. Keynes argued that a return to normal output would be slow at best, and he recommended active fiscal policy to stabilize demand and employment. His followers merged his ideas with neoclassical microeconomics into the neoclassical synthesis, which most economists accepted by the 1950s.

nature-econ-510.title: Keynes's consumption function: spending tied to today's income
nature-econ-510.text: In his 1936 General Theory, Keynes proposed a simple rule: consumer spending is a linear function of current disposable income, the income left after taxes. This consumption function is also called the absolute income hypothesis. Keynes held that real income is the most important influence on consumption in the short run. There is also a floor. Autonomous consumption is the minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing. The rule has a blind spot: it ignores future income. Its critics developed {{ref:nature-econ-513}} and {{ref:nature-econ-514}} in response.

nature-econ-502.title: The circular flow: money and goods going round
nature-econ-502.text: In 1758 François Quesnay drew the economy as a circuit in the chart described in {{ref:nature-hist-018}}, picturing an idea Richard Cantillon had described in 1730. The circular flow of income is a model showing the main exchanges in an economy as flows of money, goods and services between economic actors. Money and goods travel around a closed circuit in matching amounts but opposite directions. In the simplest version, households supply labour to businesses and spend the income they earn on the goods and services businesses produce. The model shows how activities depend on one another: without consumption there is no demand, which limits production and income. Frank Knight drew the first modern circular flow diagram in 1933. Circular flow analysis is the basis of national accounts, and so of macroeconomics.

nature-econ-500.title: Wealth versus income: the orchard and its apples
nature-econ-500.text: Picture an orchard. Wealth is like the value of the orchard on December 31, minus the debt owed on it. Income is like the value of the apples it yields each year. The first is a stock, measured at a point in time. The second is a flow, measured per unit of time. For a nation's wealth in the national accounts, the liabilities that count are those owed to the rest of the world. The two are linked by behaviour. The wealth effect is the rise in total consumption that follows a rise in national wealth.

nature-econ-521.title: Economic depreciation: the shrinking value of capital
nature-econ-521.text: Accountants depreciate an asset by spreading out its cost. Economists ask a different question: how much less are the asset's future services worth today? Economic depreciation is the gradual loss in value of a firm's or nation's capital stock through physical wear, obsolescence, or falling demand for what the capital provides. Formally, it is the fall in the present value of the services an asset will provide in future. The bookkeeping is simple. Next period's capital stock equals this period's stock plus gross investment minus depreciation, and gross investment minus depreciation is net investment. In national accounts it is called {{ref:nature-econ-517}}. Value can also rise, for example if the price of an asset's services rises unexpectedly or the discount rate falls. In the growth model of {{ref:nature-eecon-204}}, the capital stock stops changing when gross investment equals depreciation.

nature-econ-517.title: Consumption of fixed capital: the cost of wear in national accounts
nature-econ-517.text: A large cost hides inside every GDP figure. The UN manual says this cost, consumption of fixed capital, may account for 10 per cent or more of total GDP. It is the national-accounts term for depreciation: the fall in the current value of fixed assets over a period through wear, normal obsolescence and normal accidental damage. It is valued at current market prices rather than historic cost, which is why the System of National Accounts avoids the word depreciation. Subtracting it from GDP gives net domestic product, and subtracting it from {{ref:nature-econ-530}} gives {{ref:nature-econ-571}}. That net figure shows the income actually available for consumption and new investment, which makes it a better gauge of economic welfare than GDP. Some losses are left out. It excludes the using up or degradation of non-produced assets such as land, mineral deposits, coal, oil and natural gas. It also excludes assets destroyed by war or rare major natural disasters. Critics note that its economic valuation yields figures that differ from standard accounting practice.

nature-econ-494.title: Income inequality: how unevenly income is shared
nature-econ-494.text: UN Sustainable Development Goal 10 aims to reduce inequality. Income inequality is the extent to which income is spread unevenly across a population. It can be measured with tools such as the Lorenz curve and the {{ref:nature-econ-527}}. Many economists argue that some inequality is necessary, but that excessive inequality causes efficiency problems and social injustice. Globalization complicates the picture. It tends to raise a country's average income, but unequally.

nature-econ-527.title: The Gini coefficient: inequality in a single number
nature-econ-527.text: Corrado Gini published his measure in 1912, building on the work of Max Lorenz. The Gini coefficient sums up how unequally income, wealth or consumption is spread across a nation or group, from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for perfect inequality. It is usually defined from the Lorenz curve, which plots the share of total income earned by the bottom share of the population. On that chart, a straight 45-degree line means perfect equality. The simplest case shows the logic. With just two income groups, if the high earners are a share u of people and earn a share f of income, the Gini is f − u. It can be calculated on market income, before taxes and transfers, or on disposable income. UNICEF put the net income Gini of Latin America and the Caribbean at 48.3 in 2008, the highest of any region. Ecologists borrow it too, measuring biodiversity by plotting the cumulative share of species against the cumulative share of individuals.

nature-econ-488.title: What GDP leaves out
nature-econ-488.text: Robert F. Kennedy said GNP, a close cousin of GDP, measures everything except that which makes life worthwhile. Critics of GDP have a long list of reasons. It ignores negative externalities: industrial output may raise GDP while the pollution it causes goes uncounted. It excludes non-market activity such as unpaid work at home, barter and volunteer work. Estimates of unpaid work's value range from about 15% of GDP in Canada to nearly 70% in the United Kingdom. GDP also counts spending that would shrink if problems were solved, such as medical care and crime-fighting. The parable of the broken window makes the point sharply: GDP treats spending on repairs as a net benefit and ignores the original destruction. The man who developed the modern measure saw its limits. Kuznets warned in 1937 that a nation's welfare can scarcely be inferred from national income.

nature-econ-489.title: Why GDP looks good when nature suffers
nature-econ-489.text: A traffic jam is good for GDP. Stuck cars burn extra fuel, which counts as economic activity, while the resulting air pollution goes uncounted. That is the heart of the criticism: GDP rewards activities that harm the environment and fails to show natural capital being used up. Clearing forests, strip mining and taking too many fish all count as activity despite their long-term harm. GDP may not show how much natural capital an economy is building or protecting. The UK's Natural Capital Committee put it plainly in 2013. GDP focuses on flows, not stocks, so an economy can run down its assets while recording high growth. Alternatives have followed. In 1989 John Cobb and {{ref:nature-hist-040}} introduced {{ref:nature-acct-001}}, which subtracts environmental degradation and the depreciation of natural capital. In 2020 China launched {{ref:nature-acct-109}} to measure ecosystems' contribution to the economy, including its role in steadying the climate.

nature-econ-481.title: The threshold hypothesis: when more growth stops helping
nature-econ-481.text: Does more growth always mean a better life? The threshold hypothesis says no. Growth improves quality of life only up to a threshold point, after which further growth can make it worse. Plotted, the idea forms an upside-down U, whose peak marks the level of growth to aim for. Happiness has been shown to rise with GDP per person at least up to $15,000 per person. Yet health, education and political freedoms sometimes fail to improve as an economy grows.

nature-econ-555.title: Crowding out: when public spending displaces private
nature-econ-555.text: Government spending does not always add to an economy. Sometimes it just takes the place of private activity, an effect called crowding out. Full crowding out happens when government spending simply replaces private output instead of adding to it. A subtler route runs through interest rates. Government spending that raises interest rates can cut private investment, limiting what fiscal policy achieves.

nature-econ-559.title: Heterodox macroeconomics: the dissenting schools
nature-econ-559.text: Not every economist accepts the mainstream story. Heterodox macroeconomics covers the branches that reject mainstream theory, including the {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} tradition, modern monetary theory and Marxian economics. One dividing line is how prices behave. Heterodox economists see price flexibility, not price stickiness, as the source of instability, so they build models with different assumptions.

nature-econ-547.title: Monetarism: Milton Friedman's case for steady money
nature-econ-547.text: Milton Friedman updated an old idea, the quantity theory of money, and built a school of macroeconomics around it. Monetarism stresses money's role in the economy. Friedman argued that monetary policy was more effective than fiscal policy, but he favoured steady growth of the money supply over frequent intervention. With Edmund Phelps, he denied a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, a view the 1970s oil shocks supported. Monetarism was influential in the early 1980s. It faded when central banks found money growth, inflation and real GDP growth too unstably linked to target money.

nature-econ-548.title: Rational expectations: people look ahead, not just back
nature-econ-548.text: Before Robert Lucas, economists mostly assumed adaptive expectations: people forecast by looking only at the recent past. Lucas brought in rational expectations, the assumption that people use all current information about policy and conditions. The consequences were large. In new classical models with rational expectations, monetary policy had only a limited effect. The Lucas critique added that models built on past statistical relationships fail when the underlying economy changes. It called for models with microeconomic foundations instead.

nature-econ-549.title: New Keynesian economics: sticky prices bring policy back
nature-econ-549.text: New Keynesian economics accepts rational expectations but finds a way back for policy. It traces sticky prices and wages to imperfect competition, so monetary policy changes real quantities rather than only prices. Stanley Fischer and John B. Taylor showed that monetary policy could work even under rational expectations, when contracts fix wages.

nature-econ-516.title: How consumption shapes the environment
nature-econ-516.text: What people eat and wear, the homes they live in and where they shop all affect the environment. Consumption patterns changed drastically with the Industrial Revolution, as cheap mass-produced goods met rising wages. Researchers have since found affluence to be the key driver of carbon emissions. The stakes reach beyond the climate. Consuming too much, along with pollution and {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, can devastate biodiversity.

nature-econ-515.title: Household production: the economy inside the home
nature-econ-515.text: Households do not only buy things; they also make them. The New Home Economics holds that market consumption must be studied alongside the goods and services households produce for themselves. Time is the hinge. The opportunity cost of time changes the cost of home-made substitutes, and so changes the demand for bought goods and services. This home production is largely invisible in the statistics, since GDP excludes it, including unpaid childcare.

nature-econ-514.title: The life-cycle hypothesis: spending over a whole lifetime
nature-econ-514.text: Franco Modigliani argued that people do not spend according to current income alone. In his life-cycle hypothesis, people plan consumption using past, current and expected future income, spreading it over their lifetime. The source dates his publication of it to 1966. The theory grew out of criticism that the Keynesian consumption function ignores future income.

nature-econ-513.title: The permanent income hypothesis: spending on long-run income
nature-econ-513.text: Milton Friedman set out a rival idea in the 1950s, in A Theory of the Consumption Function. The permanent income hypothesis says consumption depends on a person's long-run, permanent income rather than temporary swings. Income is split into transitory and permanent parts, and changes in each affect spending differently. A change in permanent income changes consumption by the marginal propensity to consume, the share of extra income that is spent, times that change.

nature-econ-511.title: The relative income hypothesis: keeping up with others
nature-econ-511.text: In 1949 James Duesenberry argued that spending is a social act. His relative income hypothesis says people's consumption depends on their income relative to others, not only on its level. It assumes people's consumption choices are not independent of one another. So two people with the same income, but different positions in the income distribution, will consume differently.

nature-econ-533.title: Does school build skills or just signal them?
nature-econ-533.text: Does school make people more productive, or does it just reveal who already was? Human capital theory says education creates skills. In Spence and Stiglitz's signaling theory, education instead lets able workers signal their ability to employers and earn higher wages. Some labour economists criticize the Chicago-school theory for trying to explain all wage differences by human capital. Studies find wages also vary with gender, nativity, workplace discrimination and socioeconomic status. The two theories remain rival explanations of why education raises wages.
